articles.title: 324-million-year-old fossil reveals how insects conquered land
articles.summary: Ancient fossils suggest insects conquered land through a long amphibious phase rather than making an abrupt jump from water to dry ground. A newly identified 324-million-year-old species still carried paddle-like abdominal limbs, revealing an evolutionary bridge between aquatic ancestors and modern six-legged insects.
articles.content:
The rise of complex ecosystems on land was one of the major turning points in the history of life. As organisms expanded beyond the oceans, terrestrial environments became home to increasingly diverse communities. Insects, which today make up the most species-rich animal group on Earth, eventually became central to these ecosystems. Yet important parts of their early transition from water to land have remained unclear.

An international team of researchers has now identified a stem group insect from the Late Mississippian period, about 324 million years ago. By studying this fossil alongside other puzzling specimens from much earlier and later periods, the researchers reconstructed a critical stage in early insect evolution.

Their findings suggest that insects did not become fully terrestrial immediately after beginning to colonize land. Instead, early forms retained and modified features inherited from aquatic ancestors, spending an extended period in a semi-aquatic, amphibious way of life.

The research was led by Prof. Chenyang Cai of the Nanjing Institute of Geology and Paleontology of the Chinese Academy of Sciences (NIGPAS) and Erik Tihelka, a joint training Ph.D. student at the University of Cambridge. They worked with researchers from the United States, Spain, and other countries.

The findings were published in Nature on August 26.

A New Species From 324 Million Years Ago

The researchers describe a new species called Chosha praecursor. They also reexamined mysterious stem insect fossils from the Early Devonian chert deposits of Britain and the Late Carboniferous Mazon Creek biota in the United States.

Together, these fossils help close major gaps in the early history of insects. They also challenge long-standing ideas about how the insect body plan developed and how pancrustacean ancestors made the transition onto land. Most importantly, the specimens provide direct fossil evidence that the shift from aquatic to terrestrial life occurred gradually.

Molecular clock studies have suggested that hexapods split from their marine crustacean relatives and began adapting to terrestrial environments as early as the Cambrian-Ordovician interval. The fossil record, however, has told a less complete story.

Undisputed hexapod body fossils first appear in the Early Devonian Rhynie Chert around 405 million years ago. Clearly recognizable insect fossils do not become abundant until the Late Carboniferous. That leaves an approximately 80 million year gap in the fossil record.

Fossils documenting the intermediate steps have also been extremely rare. Scientists have had little direct evidence showing how early insects moved from aquatic and semi-aquatic habitats into terrestrial environments, or how their bodies changed during that process. As a result, the evolutionary path, anatomical innovations, and ecological adaptations involved in insect terrestrialization have remained poorly understood.

A Fossil Once Mistaken for a Crustacean

The newly described fossils of C. praecursor were found in calcareous claystone concretions in the Tesnus Formation of the Marathon Uplift in western Texas. They preserve unusually fine anatomical details.

Using cross-polarized light imaging, the researchers were able to identify distinctive features that revealed the fossils had been misclassified for years. Rather than crustacean larvae, the specimens were adult female insects.

The bodies measured 32.09 millimeters long. When the median caudal filament and two cerci were included, the total length reached 49.66 millimeters. Their streamlined, fusiform bodies combined features characteristic of hexapods and insects with more primitive ancestral traits.

Detailed analysis showed that C. praecursor possessed an ovipositor and a terminal caudal filament. It also had a segmented trunk and six walking legs, the basic body organization associated with insects.

But its abdomen contained something far more unusual.

Segments 1 through 9 carried segmented appendages, and the rear abdominal limbs had been modified into paddle-like structures. No living crown group insect has comparable abdominal appendages.

Geological reconstructions indicate that the sediments containing the fossils formed in near-shore, shallow-water delta coastal environments. That setting, combined with the animal's anatomy, suggests C. praecursor lived an amphibious, semi-aquatic lifestyle in humid habitats along the boundary between water and land.

Filling an 80 Million Year Gap

The team also reevaluated three enigmatic Paleozoic hexapods using detailed comparisons of their anatomy and evolutionary relationships. These included Leverhulmia from the Early Devonian of Scotland, an unnamed hexapod from the Mazon Creek biota of Illinois, USA, and C. praecursor.

The researchers concluded that all three belonged to a primitive stem lineage of insects.

Together, they represent the oldest documented assemblage of insects known so far and help fill a major missing interval in the group's evolutionary history.

The findings could significantly change how scientists understand the rise of terrestrial insects. By filling the long-standing 80 million-year hexapod gap, the work pushes the early diversification of insects back from the Late Carboniferous into the Early Devonian.

That shift brings the fossil record somewhat closer to estimates produced by molecular clock studies. The newly recognized Late Mississippian fossil also provides a valuable snapshot of an intermediate stage in insect evolution.

How Insects Lost Their Extra Limbs

The fossils shed light on another major evolutionary transformation: the emergence of the modern insect body plan.

Living hexapods have six walking legs, all attached to the thorax, while appendages on the abdomen have been almost completely lost. Paleozoic stem insects were different. Many still possessed segmented limbs along the abdomen.

The new evidence suggests that gradually reducing these abdominal appendages was an important adaptation to terrestrial life.

As insects evolved away from their crustacean ancestors, swimming appendages were progressively simplified and lost. Over time, that process produced the body arrangement familiar in modern insects.

The fossils therefore help document the anatomical transition from pancrustacean ancestors to hexapod insects.

Another important feature preserved in C. praecursor is its ovipositor. Its presence indicates that early insects had already developed different adaptations for laying eggs. Such structures could later have helped insects exploit a wide variety of terrestrial microhabitats and may have provided an anatomical foundation for their enormous later diversification.

Early Insects Lived Between Water and Land

The researchers also reconstructed how these ancient insects may have lived.

Stem group insects appear to have combined aquatic adaptations for movement and respiration with body structures increasingly suited to life on land. They probably fed on humus, decaying plant material, and fungal spores.

That would have allowed them to serve several ecological roles, including acting as decomposers and consumers in environments where aquatic and terrestrial ecosystems met. In doing so, early insects may have played an important part in the development and increasing complexity of Paleozoic land ecosystems.

The fossils of C. praecursor and related Paleozoic stem insects provide a new view of how the most species-rich animal group on Earth began its move onto land. They also challenge previous ideas about changes in insect body size, ecological adaptation, and the way insects evolved alongside terrestrial ecosystems.

Rather than making a sudden transition from water to land, insects appear to have undergone a prolonged evolutionary process. Features inherited from aquatic ancestors were retained, repurposed, simplified, and eventually lost as insects became increasingly adapted to terrestrial life.

An amphibious stage may therefore have been a crucial bridge between aquatic and fully terrestrial environments. The fossils offer new clues to the origins and early evolution of the insect body plan while also revealing how the rise of insects contributed to the emergence of increasingly complex ecosystems on land.
articles.reasoning: The article reports a significant scientific discovery about insect evolution, revealing how insects transitioned gradually from aquatic to terrestrial life. This breakthrough fills a major 80-million-year gap in the fossil record, providing valuable insights into evolutionary biology and the development of complex ecosystems on land. The research has broad scientific significance and advances understanding of a key moment in natural history.
articles.personality_title: 324-Million-Year-Old Fossil Shows How Insects Slowly Moved from Water to Land
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Insects today live mostly on land and are the most diverse group of animals. But scientists have long wondered how insects first moved from living in water to living on land. There was a big gap in fossils showing this important change.

**What happened** – Researchers found a 324-million-year-old fossil of a new insect species named Chosha praecursor in Texas. This fossil shows that early insects still had paddle-like limbs on their abdomens, which helped them live partly in water and partly on land. By studying this and other fossils from different times, scientists learned that insects spent a long time in a semi-aquatic, amphibious stage before becoming fully land animals.

**Impact** – This discovery fills an 80-million-year gap in the fossil record and changes how scientists understand insect evolution. It shows that insects did not jump suddenly from water to land but adapted slowly by keeping some water-friendly features for a long time. The fossil also explains how insects lost extra limbs on their abdomens to become the six-legged creatures we know today.

**What's next step** – Scientists will continue to study fossils like this to learn more about how insects adapted to land and how this affected early ecosystems. This research may also help explain how other animals made similar transitions from water to land.

**One-sentence takeaway** – A 324-million-year-old fossil reveals that insects moved from water to land through a long amphibious phase, gradually changing their bodies and lifestyles.
articles.personality_title_fr: Un fossile vieux de 324 millions d’années montre comment les insectes ont conquis la terre
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Aujourd’hui, les insectes vivent principalement sur terre et forment le groupe d’animaux le plus diversifié. Mais les scientifiques se demandaient depuis longtemps comment les insectes sont passés de la vie aquatique à la vie terrestre. Il y avait un grand vide dans les fossiles montrant ce changement important.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Des chercheurs ont découvert un fossile vieux de 324 millions d’années d’une nouvelle espèce d’insecte, nommée Chosha praecursor, au Texas. Ce fossile montre que les premiers insectes avaient encore des membres en forme de pagaie sur leur abdomen, ce qui leur permettait de vivre à la fois dans l’eau et sur terre. En étudiant ce fossile et d’autres d’époques différentes, les scientifiques ont appris que les insectes ont passé longtemps par une phase semi-aquatique avant de devenir complètement terrestres.

**Impact** – Cette découverte comble un vide de 80 millions d’années dans les archives fossiles et change la compréhension de l’évolution des insectes. Elle montre que les insectes ne sont pas passés soudainement de l’eau à la terre, mais ont lentement gardé des caractéristiques aquatiques. Le fossile explique aussi comment les insectes ont perdu leurs membres abdominaux supplémentaires pour devenir des créatures à six pattes.

**Prochaine étape** – Les scientifiques vont continuer à étudier des fossiles similaires pour mieux comprendre comment les insectes se sont adaptés à la terre et comment cela a influencé les premiers écosystèmes. Cette recherche pourrait aussi expliquer comment d’autres animaux ont fait ce passage de l’eau à la terre.

**Phrase clé** – Un fossile vieux de 324 millions d’années révèle que les insectes ont conquis la terre en passant par une longue phase amphibie, changeant peu à peu leur corps et leur mode de vie.
articles.personality_title_es: Fósil de 324 millones de años muestra cómo los insectos conquistaron la tierra poco a poco
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Hoy en día, los insectos viven principalmente en tierra y son el grupo de animales más diverso. Pero los científicos han querido saber cómo los insectos pasaron de vivir en el agua a vivir en tierra. Había una gran falta de fósiles que mostraran este cambio importante.

**Qué pasó** – Investigadores encontraron un fósil de 324 millones de años de una nueva especie de insecto llamada Chosha praecursor en Texas. Este fósil muestra que los primeros insectos aún tenían extremidades parecidas a palas en su abdomen, que les ayudaban a vivir en el agua y en tierra. Al estudiar este y otros fósiles de diferentes épocas, los científicos descubrieron que los insectos pasaron mucho tiempo en una etapa semiacuática antes de ser completamente terrestres.

**Impacto** – Este hallazgo llena un vacío de 80 millones de años en el registro fósil y cambia cómo los científicos entienden la evolución de los insectos. Muestra que los insectos no pasaron de agua a tierra de golpe, sino que conservaron características acuáticas por mucho tiempo. El fósil también explica cómo los insectos perdieron las extremidades extra en su abdomen para convertirse en los animales de seis patas que conocemos.

**Siguiente paso** – Los científicos seguirán estudiando fósiles como este para aprender más sobre cómo los insectos se adaptaron a la tierra y cómo esto afectó a los primeros ecosistemas. Esta investigación también podría ayudar a entender cómo otros animales hicieron cambios similares.

**Frase clave** – Un fósil de 324 millones de años revela que los insectos pasaron de agua a tierra a través de una larga etapa anfibia, cambiando poco a poco su cuerpo y forma de vida.

articles.title: What employers are looking for in the age of AI — and four ways to provide it
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 28 August 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-01913-xFor applicants whose knowledge of AI stops at the name ChatGPT, Nature spoke to academics, employers and early-career researchers to find out what you need to expand your understanding.
articles.content:
The world of artificial intelligence can be intimidating, but researchers have tips on how to get started. Credit: Jade Gao/AFP via Getty

Artificial intelligence is becoming a must-have skill for both employers and funders. Data compiled by the jobs site Indeed show that, in the United States, science jobs listing ‘AI’ as a required skill are rising sharply, whereas the overall number of science jobs has fallen (see ‘AI in demand’).

One example is the Quadram Institute in Norwich, UK, which specializes in food science and gut biology. Despite that core focus, researchers must show some knowledge of machine learning and AI, according to chief executive Daniel Figeys.

“Definitely they should be familiar with it,” he says, adding that a lot of work in Quadram’s field involves machine learning and high-throughput screening, the data from which are often analysed with AI tools. “If they were lacking all those skills, depending on the position, that would be a red flag.”

Source: Indeed

However, instead of worrying that AI systems will be taking science jobs, researchers can get ahead by using and interpreting AI tools to build their understanding. And they don’t need to know everything. Computer scientist Regina Barzilay runs a specialist course at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) in Cambridge to teach scientists AI skills. She likens it to cooking: “You don’t need to learn every recipe on Earth to feel comfortable in the kitchen … but you need to have this very basic understanding,” she says, much like “you don’t need to be a computer scientist to use a computer.”

Nature spoke to nine recruiters and researchers to ask them what the most important skills will be for scientists of all kinds in the AI era.

In short Dos and don’ts to build your AI knowledge: • Do experiment with AI technologies in your working day. • Do take a course in AI and machine learning. • Do ask AI to write code for a project, then take the code apart and learn how it works. • Don’t propose a project using AI tools without being able to show that you have the skills to back it up. • Don’t believe everything you get from a chatbot. • Don’t try to learn everything at once.

Be curious

Recruiters repeatedly told Nature that, rather than specific technical skills, they’re mostly looking for candidates who are curious to learn more about AI and are able to demonstrate that on their CVs.

“It’s the willingness to just roll up your sleeves and get into it, whether it’s informal training, whether it’s just spending some hours on open-source educational content,” explains Vijay Shah, dean of research at the Mayo Clinic in Rochester, Minnesota, which had almost 30 open research positions in May.

This is more important than specific skills, he says, because the field is moving so quickly. If you set a litmus test that requires people to be able to use AI tools such as OpenClaw or AlphaGenome, for instance, it will quickly be outdated, he adds.

It’s a sentiment echoed by Christopher Walsh, chief executive of TileBio, a start-up in Glasgow, UK, which uses AI to analyse medical images. “It’s actually really easy to teach yourself new information using large language models these days, as long as you verify the sources. So I’d recommend just having the curiosity to do that,” says Walsh. “Go and be open to learning new things, I think that’s the first step.”

Many institutions provide training in AI alongside their science curriculum, and online courses are also available, offered by institutions such as MIT and the Royal Society of Chemistry in London. “There are other ways of getting access to that type of training” rather than relying on your institution, Figeys says.

Get to know how AI thinks

One pitfall when using AI tools is putting too much faith in the results that they generate without examining the data critically. “Often it’ll give you results that it thinks you want to see, based on something you’ve said,” says Walsh. “It’s a people pleaser.”

Something that needs careful checking, according to Barzilay, is any percentage likelihood given by AI, because it might not match the observed reality. For instance, if an AI model says that there is an 80% probability that a radiology image depicts cancerous cells, “What you need to do is to say, ‘can I trust this 80%?’”

LINK Should I use AI to help draft my science job application?

This means recognizing whether the probability estimation has been calibrated against current test data to ensure its estimations match the real distributions.

For example, cancer screening models are often benchmarked against historical cases, so when these models are used to analyse new populations, the risk thresholds that they rely on might no longer match reality. In unpublished work, AI specialist Aziz Ayed and his colleagues at MIT found that the AI model MIRAI miscategorized women’s breast-cancer risk, potentially endangering lives by failing to flag some women as eligible for advanced screening.

Engineer Sydney Pham completed the machine-learning course run by Barzilay in 2024. Now working at pharmaceutical company Moderna in Cambridge, Massachusetts, she uses AI to improve manufacturing processes by working out the most promising parameters of an experiment and identifying areas for further investigation.

“Sometimes models can make sense of unexpected observations, which can guide further iterations of studies,” Pham says, but she cautions that she always corroborates AI recommendations through other means. “It’s helpful to understand how the models generate their results.”

It’s really important to get “a sense for the capabilities of the model, but also [to] develop a sense about what that means when it runs on a machine or when it interacts with data sets”, says Dominik Lukeš, a consultant at the AI Competency Centre at the University of Oxford, UK.

Because some people simply try a large language model and get “sort of wonky answers”, Lukeš thinks that it’s worth investing time in trying to understand how AI works. “There are people who’ve spent hundreds of hours learning how to take advantage of it, thinking about the process, rethinking their process and all of a sudden they will say [they] can’t live without it and ‘oh, this is an enormous game changer’.”

Know what you know

In an AI-enabled era, it feels like most research proposals are packed with ideas on how the technology can be used. However, proposal writers often don’t demonstrate that their team has the experience to implement its ideas, say hiring managers. Writing ‘we will use AI to achieve our goals’ isn’t especially credible without detail and experience to back it up.

AI features in many of the proposals that the research funder Cancer Research UK (CRUK) in London receives, says Talisia Quallo, the organization’s head of prevention and early-detection research. She says that funding committees need to see “that you understand these AI approaches and that you detail how you’re going to use them, how that algorithm works and the limitations of it”.

The production of effective humanoid robots is one research goal for some scientists working in embodied intelligence.Credit: VCG via Getty

One successful example at CRUK is Ke Yuan’s research group, called AI for Cancer Research. This team previously included Walsh, who did an undergraduate degree in computer science before specializing in cancer for his PhD.

“I was one of the members who brought computer-science knowledge,” says Walsh. Everyone had different responsibilities outlined in the grant — his role was to “translate that pathology knowledge and cell biology knowledge into code”.

Quallo says that the simplest and best way to demonstrate to evaluation committees that you know how to use AI techniques is to have publications in the field. Alternatively, she recommends including members of the project team in the grant proposal who have the relevant expertise, although every person in the team should have some knowledge of AI.
articles.reasoning: The article highlights the growing importance of AI skills in scientific research and employment, emphasizing educational initiatives and practical advice to help researchers adapt and thrive in an AI-driven era. This represents a positive real-world impact by empowering a broad range of scientists to harness AI responsibly and effectively, with significant implications for innovation and societal benefit.
articles.personality_title: How scientists can succeed by learning AI skills today
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Artificial intelligence (AI) is becoming an important skill for scientists and researchers. While some science jobs are decreasing, those requiring AI knowledge are growing quickly, especially in fields like biology and medicine.

**What happened** – Nature spoke with experts, employers, and researchers to find out what skills matter most. They shared tips like taking AI courses, experimenting with AI tools, and learning to check AI results carefully. Employers want curious learners who understand AI basics, not just experts. For example, the Quadram Institute in the UK requires researchers to know some AI because it helps analyze complex data.

**Impact** – This shows that scientists can use AI to improve their work rather than fear losing jobs to machines. Understanding AI helps researchers make better decisions and create stronger projects. For instance, at Cancer Research UK, teams succeed when members have real AI experience, making their research more credible and effective.

**What's next step** – More scientists will likely take AI training and include AI experts in their teams. As AI tools keep improving, researchers will need to stay curious and keep learning how to use AI wisely. Institutions and online platforms will continue offering courses to help with this.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Scientists who learn how AI works and use it carefully will be better prepared for future research and job opportunities.
articles.personality_title_fr: Comment les scientifiques peuvent réussir en apprenant les compétences en IA aujourd'hui

Les institutions et plateformes en ligne continueront à offrir des cours pour aider.

articles.personality_title_es: Cómo los científicos pueden tener éxito aprendiendo habilidades de IA hoy
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – La inteligencia artificial (IA) se está convirtiendo en una habilidad importante para científicos e investigadores. Mientras algunos trabajos científicos disminuyen, los que requieren conocimientos en IA aumentan rápidamente, especialmente en biología y medicina.

**Qué pasó** – Nature habló con expertos, empleadores e investigadores para saber qué habilidades son las más importantes. Compartieron consejos como tomar cursos de IA, experimentar con herramientas de IA y aprender a revisar cuidadosamente los resultados de la IA. Los empleadores buscan personas curiosas que entiendan lo básico de la IA, no solo expertos. Por ejemplo, el Instituto Quadram en el Reino Unido pide a sus investigadores que conozcan algo de IA porque ayuda a analizar datos complejos.

**Impacto** – Esto muestra que los científicos pueden usar la IA para mejorar su trabajo en vez de temer perder empleos por las máquinas. Entender la IA ayuda a los investigadores a tomar mejores decisiones y crear proyectos más fuertes. Por ejemplo, en Cancer Research UK, los equipos tienen éxito cuando sus miembros tienen experiencia real en IA, haciendo su investigación más confiable y efectiva.

Las instituciones y plataformas en línea seguirán ofreciendo cursos para ayudar.

articles.title: ‘Robot Olympics’ reveal humanoids’ rapid progress — and flaws
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 27 August 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02713-zHumanoid robots broke records at sporting events such as sprints, but struggled at practical tasks such as hammering nails.
articles.content:
Robots compete during a combat event at the second World Humanoid Robot Games in Beijing. Credit: Lintao Zhang/Getty

A human-sized robot sprinted faster than any human has before. Another jumped more than 3 metres in the air to break a record. And a third faced off against a human Olympian during a table-tennis showcase match. These were scenes from the second annual World Humanoid Robot Games in Beijing, at which robots’ physical capabilities were put to the test.

Robots run this laboratory in Japan — and are changing how scientists work

The games highlighted how fast humanoid robots — which use artificial intelligence to learn, plan and execute real-world actions — are advancing. But they also demonstrated that the machines have a long way to go before they’ll be used by humans for practical tasks.

“If I ask you which is harder — folding laundry or doing a backflip — most people will say folding laundry is way easier,” says Karen Liu, a computer scientist at Stanford University in California. “But for humanoids, doing a task that we do in our daily lives is actually way harder than a backflip.”

This year’s games — which ran from 22 to 26 August and drew more than 600 competing teams, mainly from Chinese universities, research institutions and robotics companies — expanded the competition from sprints and jumps to include real-world challenges such as shelving books and making beds. In these ‘scenario-based events’, which started before the athletics competitions, robots that completed tasks on their own were scored more highly than those that were remotely operated by humans.

The games “are not simply a competition, but an important real-world testing ground for embodied intelligence”, says Cheng Hao, chief executive of Booster Robotics in Beijing, which had nearly 300 robots at the games.

This video from the Associated Press shows scenes from the second World Humanoid Robot Games in Beijing, along with interviews of some of the research team members competing there. Credit: Associated Press

The event’s emphasis on practical tasks is crucial for developing useful robots, says Aya Durbin, who directs development of the Atlas humanoid robot at Boston Dynamics in Waltham, Massachusetts, which did not send robots to the games. “Humanoids won’t become a part of our everyday lives if they’re always ‘toys’. They need to be used to solve actual problems and make the world a better place.”

Strengths and weaknesses

During the games, a robot from company X-Humanoid in Beijing took home a gold medal in the 100-metre sprint with a time of 8.64 seconds — almost one second faster than Olympian Usain Bolt’s record-breaking race in 2009. The same robot won the 100-metre sprint last year in 21.5 seconds, showing how quickly the technology is advancing. Another X-Humanoid bot jumped 3.4 metres vertically from a standing position at this year’s games, breaking a human record set in 1993, according to the state-run Chinese news outlet the Global Times.

Humanoids thrive in track-and-field events because they translate energy into acceleration extremely efficiently, Liu says. Backflips and sprints are actions that follow a prescribed trajectory for robots, she says. “Every single millisecond, it knows what to do and how much torque to generate. It doesn’t need to ‘think’.”

In this video from state-run Chinese video news agency CCTV+, robots hammer nails into a board during one event at the games with varying degrees of success. Credit: CCTV+

What humanoids struggle with is high-dexterity tasks, Liu continues. Creating robotic ‘grippers’ that can mimic the strength and coordination of the human hand is challenging, she says, and using tools is particularly hard for the bots because grippers struggle to create enough contact with a tool to apply strong force.

Indeed, robots at the games struggled to hammer nails into a corkboard efficiently, even when operated by team members wearing gloves that control the robots’ movements.
articles.reasoning: The article reports on significant advancements in humanoid robot capabilities demonstrated at the World Humanoid Robot Games, highlighting rapid progress in physical performance such as sprinting and jumping that surpass human records. It also emphasizes the importance of practical, real-world tasks for future robot utility, showing meaningful progress with broad implications for robotics technology and its potential societal benefits. The detailed coverage of the event and its impact on embodied intelligence research provides substantial context.
articles.personality_title: Humanoid robots break records and face new challenges at World Robot Games
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – The World Humanoid Robot Games is an annual event where robots that look and move like humans compete in various physical and practical tasks. This year’s competition took place in Beijing and included over 600 teams mostly from China.

**What happened** – Robots set new records in sports events, including a robot sprinting 100 meters faster than the fastest human ever and another jumping over 3 meters high. They also competed in everyday tasks like shelving books and hammering nails. While robots excelled in running and jumping, they found tasks requiring fine hand movements, like hammering nails, much harder.

**Impact** – These results show how quickly robot technology is improving in some areas, especially in fast, repeated movements. But they also reveal that robots still struggle with tasks that need careful hand control and tool use. This helps scientists understand where to focus their work to build robots that can help people in daily life.

**What's next step** – Researchers will continue to improve robot hands and their ability to use tools. Future competitions will likely test these skills more, moving robots closer to being useful helpers in homes and workplaces.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Humanoid robots are breaking physical records but need better hand skills to handle everyday tasks, guiding future improvements in robotics technology.
articles.personality_title_fr: Les robots humanoïdes battent des records et relèvent de nouveaux défis aux Jeux mondiaux des robots
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Les Jeux mondiaux des robots humanoïdes sont un événement annuel où des robots ressemblant et bougeant comme des humains s’affrontent dans diverses épreuves sportives et pratiques. Cette année, la compétition a eu lieu à Pékin avec plus de 600 équipes, principalement chinoises.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Des robots ont établi de nouveaux records sportifs, notamment un robot courant 100 mètres plus vite que l’humain le plus rapide et un autre sautant plus de 3 mètres de haut. Ils ont aussi participé à des tâches quotidiennes comme ranger des livres et enfoncer des clous. Si les robots ont excellé dans la course et le saut, ils ont eu du mal avec des tâches demandant une grande précision manuelle, comme enfoncer des clous.

**Impact** – Ces résultats montrent que la technologie des robots progresse rapidement pour les mouvements rapides et répétitifs, mais que la maîtrise des gestes fins reste un défi. Cela aide les scientifiques à mieux cibler leurs recherches pour créer des robots capables d’aider au quotidien.

**Prochaines étapes** – Les chercheurs vont continuer à améliorer les mains des robots et leur capacité à utiliser des outils. Les futures compétitions testeront probablement davantage ces compétences, rapprochant les robots d’une utilisation pratique dans les foyers et les lieux de travail.

**Résumé en une phrase** – Les robots humanoïdes battent des records physiques mais doivent améliorer leur dextérité pour accomplir les tâches quotidiennes, ce qui guidera les avancées futures en robotique.
articles.personality_title_es: Robots humanoides rompen récords y enfrentan nuevos retos en los Juegos Mundiales de Robots
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Los Juegos Mundiales de Robots Humanoides son un evento anual donde robots que se parecen y se mueven como humanos compiten en actividades deportivas y tareas prácticas. Este año, la competencia se realizó en Pekín con más de 600 equipos, principalmente de China.

**Qué pasó** – Los robots establecieron nuevos récords deportivos, incluyendo uno que corrió 100 metros más rápido que el humano más rápido y otro que saltó más de 3 metros de altura. También participaron en tareas cotidianas como ordenar libros y martillar clavos. Aunque los robots destacaron en correr y saltar, tuvieron dificultades con tareas que requieren movimientos finos de las manos, como martillar clavos.

**Impacto** – Estos resultados muestran que la tecnología de robots avanza rápido en movimientos rápidos y repetitivos, pero el control fino de las manos sigue siendo un reto. Esto ayuda a los científicos a enfocar mejor sus investigaciones para crear robots que puedan ayudar en la vida diaria.

**Próximo paso** – Los investigadores seguirán mejorando las manos de los robots y su capacidad para usar herramientas. Es probable que futuras competencias pongan a prueba estas habilidades, acercando a los robots a ser útiles en hogares y lugares de trabajo.

**Resumen en una frase** – Los robots humanoides están rompiendo récords físicos pero necesitan mejorar su destreza manual para realizar tareas cotidianas, lo que guiará los avances futuros en tecnología robótica.

articles.title: Healed fang wound found on 520-million-year-old apex predator
articles.summary: Something took a bite out of one of the biggest predators in Cambrian seas, an extraordinary fossil shows – and it could well be cannibalism
articles.content:
Something took a bite out of one of the biggest predators in Cambrian seas, an extraordinary fossil shows – and it could well be cannibalism

Artist’s drawing of Amplectobelua symbrachiata, a Cambrian Period apex predator Yu Wu, Northwest University, Xi'an, China

Even top predators weren’t safe in Cambrian seas around 520 million years ago. An extraordinary fossil shows a healed wound where one predator took a bite out of the side of another.

“I would never have expected to see something like this preserved in the fossil record,” says Stephen Pates at University College London.

The predator with a bite taken out of it is called Amplectobelua symbrachiata, which belonged to a long-extinct group of strange arthropods known as the radiodonts that looked a bit like a cross between squid and lobsters. They had two vicious, grasping appendages on their heads for catching prey, and a line of swimming flaps protruding from their sides that decreased in size towards their rear.

Advertisement

They grew to nearly a metre long, which might be tiny compared with modern marine predators, but back in the Cambrian Period, it made them one of the biggest predators around.

The swimming flaps of radiodonts were softer than their grasping appendages, resulting in very few fossils of them. But a team recently found a single flap at a site in China called the Yu’anshan Formation, where soft tissues are exceptionally preserved.

It is recognisable as a radiodont flap because of a characteristic pattern of lines on its surface. If it was the largest swimming flap, the animal would have been at least 23 centimetres long. If it was one of the smaller flaps, it could have been much larger.

Subscriber-only newsletter Sign up to Editor’s Highlights Sign up to newsletter

The researchers noticed an odd W-shaped feature on the edge of the flap – the kind of shape typically left when two fangs tear through flesh.

But is it really a bite wound? The researchers in China got in touch with Pates because he has studied similar injuries in trilobites. “You want to rule out that it’s been broken during the fossilisation process,” says Pates.

X-ray fluorescence mapping shows that the chemical composition of the W-shaped part is consistent with the rest of the fossil, which means it’s not an artefact caused by flaking. “This is telling us that this is likely a flap that was preserved like this, rather than altered later,” says Pates.

A possible wound in the Cambrian fossil Kunsheng Du and Wei Li

What’s more, there is a black band visible around the edges of the W-shape that appears to be a sign of healing. “In modern arthropods, you see this melanisation, this darkening around areas where they’re regrowing,” he says. “I think we can be fairly confident this happened while the animal was alive.”

It is an extraordinary find because only around 10 isolated radiodont flaps like this have ever been found, says Pates. “With more complete specimens, even if these wounds were there, you wouldn’t necessarily be able to see them.”

So, what took a chunk out of this ancient predator? The team can’t be sure, but it could have been another species of radiodont, or even a member of the same species, says Pates.

Hundreds of likely predation wounds have been found on trilobites, but their fossils are much more common because of their hard exoskeletons and because they survived until 250 million years ago, whereas radiodonts were all extinct by around 480 million years ago. Trilobites were also much smaller and nearer the bottom of the food chain.

“There have been other reports of healed injuries in Cambrian animals, though never in a radiodont,” says Joe Moysiuk at the Manitoba Museum in Canada. “With only one specimen, I don’t think we can rule out other potential causes.”

For instance, it’s not unusual for arthropods to suffer injuries while shedding an exoskeleton, and so this flap might have been damaged during moulting, says Moysiuk.

“You can’t rule it out, but it’s [a] balance of probabilities,” says Pates. For instance, a moulting wound is most likely to be a singular tear, whereas the W-shape points more towards a bite mark, he says. The location on the flap is also what would be expected if the radiodont was fleeing an attacker, whereas a moulting wound could occur anywhere on the animal’s body.

“For us, the best interpretation for this injury is a predation injury,” says Pates.
articles.reasoning: The discovery of a healed bite wound on a 520-million-year-old apex predator fossil provides a significant scientific breakthrough in understanding ancient marine ecosystems and predator-prey interactions. This finding offers new insights into Cambrian period life and fossil preservation, which has broad implications for paleontology and evolutionary biology.
articles.personality_title: Scientists find healed bite wound on 520-million-year-old sea predator fossil
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Around 520 million years ago, during the Cambrian Period, the seas were home to strange creatures called radiodonts. These were early predators that looked like a mix of squids and lobsters. One of the largest was Amplectobelua symbrachiata, nearly a meter long and a top hunter of its time.

**What happened** – Researchers discovered a rare fossil in China that shows a healed bite wound on the swimming flap of an Amplectobelua symbrachiata. The flap had a clear W-shaped mark, likely made by sharp fangs, and a dark band around it that suggests the wound was healing while the animal was still alive. X-ray tests confirmed the mark was not caused by damage after the fossil formed.

**Impact** – This is the first time a healed injury has been found on a radiodont fossil. It gives scientists new evidence that even the biggest predators back then faced attacks, possibly from other predators or even their own kind. The fossil also helps us understand how ancient sea creatures could survive injuries and how fossils can preserve such detailed stories.

**What's next step** – Scientists will keep searching for more fossils with signs of injuries to learn how common these battles were in ancient seas. They also want to study more about how these early animals healed and what this means for the evolution of predator-prey relationships.

**One-sentence takeaway** – A rare fossil shows that 520 million years ago, even top sea predators survived attacks and healed from their wounds, revealing new details about ancient marine life and survival.
articles.personality_title_fr: Une blessure cicatrisée découverte sur un fossile de prédateur marin vieux de 520 millions d’années
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Il y a environ 520 millions d’années, durant la période cambrienne, les mers abritaient des créatures étranges appelées radiodontes. Ces prédateurs anciens ressemblaient à un mélange de calmars et de homards. L’un des plus grands, Amplectobelua symbrachiata, mesurait près d’un mètre et était un chasseur de premier plan.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Des chercheurs ont découvert un fossile rare en Chine montrant une blessure cicatrisée par morsure sur un aileron natatoire d’Amplectobelua symbrachiata. L’aileron portait une marque en forme de W, probablement causée par des crocs pointus, ainsi qu’une bande sombre autour, signe que la blessure guérissait de son vivant. Des tests aux rayons X ont confirmé que la marque n’était pas due à des dommages postérieurs à la fossilisation.

**Impact** – C’est la première fois qu’une blessure cicatrisée est trouvée sur un fossile de radiodonte. Cela montre que même les plus grands prédateurs de l’époque subissaient des attaques, peut-être d’autres prédateurs ou même de leur propre espèce. Ce fossile aide aussi à comprendre comment ces animaux anciens pouvaient survivre à leurs blessures et comment les fossiles peuvent raconter des histoires aussi précises.

**Prochaines étapes** – Les scientifiques chercheront d’autres fossiles avec des signes de blessures pour savoir à quelle fréquence ces combats avaient lieu dans les mers anciennes. Ils veulent aussi étudier la guérison de ces animaux et ce que cela signifie pour l’évolution des relations entre prédateurs et proies.

**Résumé en une phrase** – Un fossile rare montre que, il y a 520 millions d’années, même les plus grands prédateurs marins survivaient aux attaques et guérissaient, révélant de nouveaux détails sur la vie marine ancienne et la survie.
articles.personality_title_es: Descubren herida cicatrizada en fósil de depredador marino de 520 millones de años
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Hace unos 520 millones de años, durante el período Cámbrico, los mares estaban habitados por criaturas extrañas llamadas radiodontos. Eran depredadores antiguos que parecían una mezcla entre calamares y langostas. Uno de los más grandes, Amplectobelua symbrachiata, medía casi un metro y era un cazador principal.

**Qué pasó** – Investigadores encontraron un fósil raro en China que muestra una herida cicatrizada por mordedura en una aleta natatoria de Amplectobelua symbrachiata. La aleta tenía una marca en forma de W, probablemente hecha por colmillos afilados, y una banda oscura alrededor que indica que la herida estaba sanando mientras el animal vivía. Pruebas con rayos X confirmaron que la marca no fue causada por daños después de la fosilización.

**Impacto** – Es la primera vez que se encuentra una herida cicatrizada en un fósil de radiodonto. Esto demuestra que incluso los depredadores más grandes de esa época sufrían ataques, posiblemente de otros depredadores o incluso de su propia especie. El fósil también ayuda a entender cómo estos animales antiguos podían sobrevivir a heridas y cómo los fósiles pueden conservar detalles tan precisos.

**Próximo paso** – Los científicos seguirán buscando más fósiles con señales de heridas para aprender con qué frecuencia ocurrían estas peleas en los mares antiguos. También quieren estudiar cómo sanaban estos animales y qué significa esto para la evolución de las relaciones entre depredadores y presas.

**Conclusión en una frase** – Un fósil raro revela que hace 520 millones de años, incluso los principales depredadores marinos sobrevivían a ataques y sanaban sus heridas, mostrando nuevos detalles sobre la vida marina antigua y la supervivencia.
